In a D&D campaign I DMed a few years ago, the main artefact was a multidimensional prison shaped as a Rubik's cube. It had to be manipulated from time to time to prevent the entities imprisoned inside from "solving" it and breaking free.

But in this case, I think the cube is also symbolic of her mind and multiple personalities - she is unstable, a creature from a future that doesn't exist anymore, with a "dark" twin inside her head, maybe more "facets" even. Maybe the cube is a way to symbolize her constant work to keep herself "whole" rather than dissolving as the living paradox she has become ?

posts.name: jagarciao
posts.cooked:
I just watched Man of Steel last night and couldn't help but think that Superman was probably not very popular after that movie. The bad guys (as far as everyone is concerned) came to Earth for no other reason than to get him, so he was in essence a solution to a problem he created. Also, he kept throwing the bad guys into buildings and other populated locations at times and in ways that seemed unnecessarily destructive... yes, he may have saved the planet but did it have to be done in a manner that cost those people their lives? I would imagine the family and loved ones of the deceased would not be as quick to hold him in high regard. 

I imagine superheroes overall wouldn't be held in as high regard by the public as we might imagine... especially if they are given free reign to operate above the law.  I think in fact a very large and vocal group would demand that the government keep the FV accountable. And whether or not they were able to, they would have to at least make a show of it. Bunker suits with anti-FV capabilities would be made and pilots would be trained by this time and a network of spies dedicated to knowing exactly where the FV members were at all times. 

We have seen how arms races play out in a world and I imagine superheroes would shape the geopolitical discourse in a very similar manner... and no one likes to see such powerful weapons in the hands of independent interests.

posts.name: Ironic
posts.cooked:
I am clearly in the minority, but I just cannot comprehend the government being described as increasingly hardline, restrictive, uncooperative, etc... up until the heroes stop taking orders entirely.  But as soon as the group of human superweapons goes rogue, then they're totally okay with it and there's no conflict at all.

There are superhero setting governments which try to control the heroes to the point it ties their hands, and there are superhero setting governements who let heroes do their thing, either out of legitimate trust or simply the need to keep up appearances.  That one government could fit into both groups at once is utterly baffling to me.

But I think I now see the answer: the government's true restrictions were fashion-related.  For years, the Freedom Five And Also These Other Three Ladies Who Don't Get Counted I Guess wanted desperately to have grey panels on the sides of their costumes, wear matching belt buckles, and paint the Bunker suit in patches of rust orange, but The Man wouldn't let them.  However, now that they are no longer defined as a costumed service, the FV are beyond the reach of the jack-booted fashion police, and can fly free!

It's really quite uplifting.

Many things have changed in the last several years. After some of the major, nigh existence-ending events which rocked our world, there was backlash against superpowered individuals, and the U.S. government sought to gain tighter control of their superteam, The Freedom Five. A series of mandates left the team unable to act without court permission and hamstrung their ability to fight villains on non-U.S. soil.
